text:
Whether Monzo’s paid plans are worth it depends heavily on your lifestyle, habits, and whether you would actually pay for the included services separately.

Monzo offers three paid tiers: **Extra** (£3/mo), **Perks** (£9/mo), and **Max** (£19/mo). Monzo’s **free account** already covers the essentials (pots, bill-splitting, instant notifications, and fee-free spending abroad).

---

### 1. Monzo Extra (£3/month = £36/year)
* **What you get:** Power-user budgeting tools. Connect external bank accounts/credit cards into the Monzo app, live auto-export transactions to Google Sheets, custom spending categories, virtual cards, and enhanced credit score tracking.
* **Is it worth it?**
  * **Yes, if:** You are a budgeting enthusiast who heavily relies on spreadsheets or you frequently shop online and want virtual cards linked directly to specific spending pots.
  * **No, if:** You just want basic budgeting. Standalone open-banking budgeting apps (like Snoop or free tiers of Emma) and rivals like Chase UK (which offers multiple sub-accounts with separate card details) provide similar features for free.

---

### 2. Monzo Perks (£9/month = £108/year)
* **What you get:** Everything in *Extra*, plus lifestyle rewards:
  * A **weekly Greggs treat** (hot drink, sausage roll, sweet treat, etc.)
  * A **free annual National Railcard** (worth £30–£35)
  * A boosted interest rate on Instant Access Savings
  * 3 free cash deposits a year at PayPoints and higher international ATM limits
* **Is it worth it?**
  * **Yes, if:** You regularly buy train tickets and pass a Greggs. If you claim the Railcard (~£35/year) and pick up a Greggs treat even twice a month (~£40–£50/year in value), you recoup most of the annual fee.
